sections.title: Fundamental Definitions & Waveforms
content: Definition: An involuntary, rhythmic, biphasic oscillation of the eyes. A sign of ocular motor instability, not a diagnosis.
Jerk Nystagmus: Slow-phase drift from visual target followed by a fast-phase corrective saccade. Named after the fast phase.
Pendular Nystagmus: Back-and-forth slow-phase movements of equal velocity in each direction; no fast phase.
Pathological nystagmus: Involuntary defoveating movement followed by refixating saccade. The slow phase indicates the pathology.

sections.title: The DWARF Mnemonic: Clinical Features Assessment

content.explanation: D: Direction (Horizontal, vertical, torsional, mixed). W: Waveform (Jerk vs. Pendular). A: Amplitude/Frequency (Fine/coarse, High/Low). R: Rest/Gaze (Primary position vs. eccentric gaze). F: Fixation (Dampens in peripheral vestibular; increases in congenital).

sections.title: Workup Mind Map: The Diagnostic Approach

branches: Initial History: Onset (Early vs. Acquired), Oscillopsia (absent in congenital), Associated Symptoms (Vertigo, ataxia, motor weakness)
Physical Exam: Null Point (minimal intensity position), Convergence effect, Monocular occlusion (latent component), OKN testing (paradoxical reversal)
Investigations: Neuroimaging (MRI mandatory for See-saw, Downbeat, Gaze-evoked), Electrophysiology (ERG/VEP for sensory causes like LCA/Achromatopsia)
Systemic Review: Check for Wernicke risk, drug/toxin screens (Alcohol, Phenytoin, Lithium)
Cerebellar Testing: Gait (ataxia), Rapid alternating movements (dysdiadochokinesia), Tremors

sections.title: High-Yield Clinical Scenarios (1-5)
content: Scenario 1: Paradoxical OKN Reversal (eyes move in opposite direction of stripes). Pathognomonic for INS; seen in 60-66% of patients. Uniplanar, dampens with convergence, abolished during sleep.

Scenario 2: Latent Nystagmus (FMNS). Right eye covered = left-beating jerk (beats toward fixing eye). Associated with infantile esotropia. Measurement pitfall: Use fogging (plus lenses), not total occlusion.
Scenario 3: Physiological End-point. Fine jerk at >45° gaze. Pathologic ONLY if persistent, large-amplitude, or asymmetric.
Scenario 4: Asymmetric Gaze-evoked. Large amplitude to right, absent to left. Suggests ipsilateral brainstem/cerebellum lesion (stroke, tumor, MS). MRI mandatory.

Scenario 5: Bruns Nystagmus (CPA Tumor/Acoustic Neuroma). Ipsilateral gaze: Large amplitude, low frequency (brainstem compression). Contralesional gaze: Small amplitude, high frequency (vestibular nerve damage).

sections.title: High-Yield Clinical Scenarios (6-10)
content: Scenario 6: Alexander's Law (Peripheral Vestibular). Intensity increases as eyes move toward fast-beating component. Dampened by visual fixation; improves over weeks.
Scenario 7: Spasmus Nutans Syndrome. Triad: Shimmering nystagmus + Head nodding + Torticollis. Mimics chiasmal/suprasellar gliomas. MRI mandatory.
Scenario 8: Periodic Alternating Nystagmus (PAN). Horizontal jerk beats right for 90s, pause 10s, beats left 90s. Treatment: Baclofen (5–10 mg TID).
Scenario 9: Rebound Nystagmus. Brief nystagmus in opposite direction after returning to center from eccentric gaze. Manifestation of cerebellar disease.
Scenario 10: Caloric Testing (COWS). Cold water = Opposite beating; Warm water = Same beating. In comatose patient: Cold causes slow phase deviation TOWARD irrigated side only.

sections.title: High-Yield Clinical Scenarios (11-15)
content: Scenario 11: Oscillopsia. Illusion of environmental movement. DDx: Acquired jerk (Up/Downbeat), INO, Myasthenia, SOM. Notably absent in congenital cases due to neural damping.
Scenario 12: Sensory Deprivation. Bilateral cataracts = searching, roving eye movements. If vision poor under 2 years, nystagmus becomes irreversible. Often pendular in primary.
Scenario 13: Toxic Integrator Leak (Drug-induced). Phenytoin, barbiturates, alcohol. Toxic effect on neural integration structures (brainstem/cerebellum).
Scenario 14: Acquired Pendular (MS). Asymmetric, high-frequency sinusoidal movements. Treatment: Gabapentin (300–600 mg TID) or Memantine (10–20 mg QD).
Scenario 15: Nystagmus Blockage Syndrome. Child uses active convergence/adduction to damp nystagmus, causing manifest esotropia. Intensity inversely proportional to ET angle.

rows: Repositions muscles to shift null point to primary position.
Occasionally used for PAN or severe nystagmus.

branches: Definition: Elevation/Intorsion in one eye, simultaneous Depression/Extorsion in the fellow eye.
Localization: Rostral midbrain, Diencephalon, or Suprasellar region (Craniopharyngioma).
Acquired vs. Pseudo: Acquired (stroke/trauma); Pseudo (Jerk-like, localized to medulla).
Management: Surgical treatment of tumor; Baclofen for oscillopsia.
DDx: Spasmus Nutans (benign shimmer) vs. Chiasmal Tumor (Seesaw).
Sign comparison vs. OTR: Seesaw is rhythmic; Ocular Tilt Reaction (OTR) is a static deviation.

sections.title: Red Flag Clinical Associations
content: Seesaw + Bitemporal hemianopia = Suprasellar Tumor until proven otherwise.
Sudden Seesaw + Severe Headache = Pituitary Apoplexy.
Vertical Nystagmus (Up/Downbeat) = Mandatory MRI Brain/Orbits.
Monocular shimmering nystagmus = Rule out Optic Pathway Glioma.
Child with nystagmus + small eye + cataract = Check for ON Hypoplasia/Foveal Hypoplasia.
Nystagmus not suppressed by fixation = Central Vestibular Disorder.

rows: Fast phase beats down. Accentuated in downgaze.
Medulla or anterior cerebellar vermis (MS, Stroke, Wernicke, Smoking).

sections.title: Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia (INO) & Ataxic Nystagmus
content: Description: Limitation of adduction in ipsilateral eye.
Nystagmus: Horizontal jerk nystagmus of the contralateral abducting eye.
Term: Ataxic Nystagmus.
Mechanism: Increased neural pulsing to overcome adduction weakness.
Localization: Lesion of the Medial Longitudinal Fasciculus (MLF).

rows: Intermittent, purely horizontal saccades; no intersaccadic interval.

sections.title: Pediatric Case: Cataract, Nystagmus & Microcornea
content: Assessment: Check for ON Hypoplasia, Foveal Hypoplasia, Iris Coloboma (incomplete fetal fissure closure).
Visual Prognosis: Presence of nystagmus suggests poorer prognosis. VA often <6/60 in Albinism due to foveal hypoplasia.
Surgical Risks: Zonular Dialysis (capsular tension ring needed). Weak zonules increase PCR risk.
Small Eye Challenges: Microcornea complicates IOL power calculation; AC crowding requires high-viscosity viscoelastics.
Timing: Bilateral dense cataracts need surgery within first 10 weeks of life.
Genetic Testing: Consider FRMD7-associated INS.

sections.title: Albinism-Associated Nystagmus
content: Waveform: Pendular and horizontal.
Light Effect: Nystagmus increases in bright illumination.
VA: Typically 6/36–6/60 (stationary, not progressive).
Cause: Foveal hypoplasia.

sections.title: Additional Neuro-Oph VIVA Facts
sections.content: Foster Kennedy Syndrome (Anosmia scenario): Triad of ipsilateral optic atrophy, contralateral papilledema, and anosmia; typically frontal lobe mass. Heimann-Bielschowsky Phenomenon: Monocular vertical pendular oscillations in an eye with long-standing poor vision. Superior Oblique Myokymia (SOM): Monocular, high-frequency SO contraction bursts; treated with Carbamazepine. Syringobulbia: Extension of syrinx into brainstem; can cause acquired seesaw nystagmus.
